turns.user: my carry-on got flagged at the gate for being too big. i thought it was under the limit but the bag is 22 inches tall with the wheels. why does it matter if the wheels count? i want to understand the rules so i don't get caught on the return flight
turns.assistant:
Airlines measure the bag's total outer dimensions, and wheels, handles and side pockets all count. The gauge at the gate is a fixed frame, and the bag has to fit inside it without forcing. That's why a bag that looks fine on the floor can fail.

The reason for the strictness is overhead bin space. If every bag is slightly oversized, the bins fill up and more people have to check bags at the gate, which costs the airline and delays boarding. So the rules are enforced by the frame rather than by eye.

For the return flight, measure the bag yourself with the wheels on and the handle down, at its tallest and widest points. Then check the exact limit on the airline's own website, since the numbers differ by carrier and some are slightly smaller than the common 22 x 14 x 9 inch standard.

turns.user: so the wheels count? i figured they weren't part of the size. and why do some airlines let the same bag through and others don't
turns.assistant:
Yes, the wheels count, usually as part of the height. Most people forget that and only measure the body of the bag.

As for why it varies: each airline sets its own limit, and the enforcement depends on the flight. On a half-empty plane, the gate agent may not check at all. On a full flight with tight bins, they'll gauge every bag. Some carriers also allow a small tolerance and others are strict. So the same bag can pass one day and get flagged the next.

If your bag is close to the limit, pick a carry-on that's a bit under the maximum on the airline's page. That gives you margin for overpacking, and a tape measure in your bag will tell you the truth before you get to the gate.

Yes. The gravity component along the slope is mg sin(30°), so with F = ma the mass cancels out:

a = g sin(30°) = 9.81 × 0.5 ≈ 4.9 m/s²

The 5 kg doesn't change the result. A 50 kg block on the same frictionless incline accelerates at the same rate. The mass only matters for the force, not the acceleration.

turns.user: Quick question on essays: is it ok to use 'I' in an argumentative essay for a college class? My prof said first person is fine in one, but my TA said to avoid it.
turns.assistant:
It depends on the discipline and the instructor. In many humanities classes, 'I' is fine when you're stating your position, as in 'I argue that...', because it makes the claim clear and owns it. Personal anecdotes need more care, and they should earn their place by supporting the argument.

In science or social science writing, the convention is often to avoid first person. Since your prof and TA disagree, check the assignment rubric or ask which one grades the essay. If the rubric doesn't mention it, a safe middle ground is to use 'I' sparingly, mainly for the thesis.

turns.user: what about 'we' as in 'we can see that'
turns.assistant: I'd avoid it. 'We' can sound like you're speaking for the reader, and it often hides who did the analysis. 'The data show' or 'the text suggests' is more precise. If you want a subject for the action, 'I' works better than 'we' in a single-author essay, since you're the one making the claim.

turns.user: ok and do i need a works cited for a 1000 word essay with 3 sources
turns.assistant:
Yes. Any source you quote, paraphrase or draw an idea from needs an in-text citation, and each source goes on the works cited page. Three sources is still three sources, so the list is required even for a short essay.

Check which style your class uses. MLA is common in English and humanities, and APA in psychology and social sciences. The format for each citation differs, so use the rubric or a citation generator and double-check the output against the style guide.

turns.user: does the works cited page count toward the 1000 words
turns.assistant:
Usually not. Both MLA and APA exclude the works cited or reference list from the word count, but in-text citations count as part of the text. Title pages and headers are normally excluded too.

Since word limits vary, check whether your instructor specifies what's included. If the assignment just says 1000 words, a good rule is to aim for 1000 words in the body and count the works cited separately.

turns.user: thanks. one more, is a conclusion supposed to introduce new info or just restate
turns.assistant:
It should mostly synthesize rather than restate or introduce new evidence. Restating your thesis word for word is weak, so rephrase it in light of what you've shown. Then explain why it matters: what follows from the argument, what it changes, or what question is still open.

Bringing in a brand-new source or example in the conclusion usually makes the argument feel unfinished, so put that material in the body instead. A small new idea that follows logically from your argument is fine if it helps the reader see the bigger picture.

turns.user:
why does a LEFT JOIN with a WHERE clause on the right table act like an inner join? i ran this and got fewer rows than i expected and i don't get why

SELECT s.name, c.title
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id
LEFT JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
WHERE c.title = 'Biology'
turns.assistant:
The LEFT JOIN keeps every student, including students with no enrollments, and fills the course columns with NULL for them. But the WHERE clause runs after the join. For a student with no classes, c.title is NULL, and NULL = 'Biology' evaluates to unknown, not true. So those rows get filtered out, and the result looks like an inner join.

If you want all students and only the Biology enrollments attached to them, move the condition into the ON clause:

```
SELECT s.name, c.title
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id
LEFT JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id AND c.title = 'Biology'
```

Now the condition only decides which course rows get matched. Students who don't match still come through, with NULL in the title column.

turns.user: so if i put the condition in the on clause it keeps the students with no biology class? what would the nulls look like
turns.assistant:
Yes. Every student appears at least once. Students with a Biology enrollment show the title, and everyone else shows NULL in that column:

```
name      | title
----------+----------
Alice     | Biology
Ben       | NULL
Chen      | Biology
Dara      | NULL
```

If a student took several courses, they'll appear once per matching row, so you may still see duplicates for students with multiple Biology enrollments. If you only want each student once, use DISTINCT or a subquery that checks for the course, rather than joining the table at all.
